nodes.name: Euclidean distance and Lebesgue measure on R^d
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $\mathbb{R}^d$ be the Euclidean vector space equipped with distance $\|\cdot\|$ and Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(\cdot)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Open ball B_d(x,r)
nodes.statement: For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ we denote by $B_d(x,r)$ the open ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with center $x$ and radius $r$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Sphere packing
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a discrete set of points such that $\|x-y\|\geq2$ for any distinct $x,y\in X$. Then the union $$\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{x\in X} B_d(x,1)$$ is a \emph{sphere packing}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Lattice sphere packing
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a lattice in $\mathbb{R}^d$ then we say that $\mathcal{P}$ is a \emph{lattice sphere packing}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Finite density of a packing
nodes.statement: The \emph{finite density} of a packing $\mathcal{P}$ is defined as $$\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(r):=\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{P}\cap B_d(0,r))}{\mathrm{Vol}(B_d(0,r))},\quad r>0.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(r)$: fraction of the ball $B_d(0,r)$ covered by the packing.

nodes.name: Density of a packing
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{density} of a packing $\mathcal{P}$ as the limit superior $$\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}:=\limsup\limits_{r\to\infty}\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(r). $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Density $\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}$ = limsup of the finite density as $r\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Sphere packing constant Delta_d
nodes.statement: The number be want to know is the supremum over all possible packing densities $$\Delta_d:=\sup\limits_{\substack{\mathcal{P}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\\ \scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{sphere}\;\mathrm{packing}}}\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}, $$ called the \emph{sphere packing constant}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Delta_1 = 1
nodes.statement: Trivially, in dimension~$1$ we have $\Delta_1=1$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: $\Delta_1=1$

nodes.name: Optimality of the hexagonal packing in dimension 2 (Thue; Fejes Toth)
nodes.statement: It has long been known that a best packing in dimension $2$ is the familiar hexagonal lattice packing, in which each disk is touching six others.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: a best packing in dimension $2$ is the familiar hexagonal lattice packing

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture
nodes.statement: Johannes Kepler conjectured in his essay ``On the six-cornered snowflake'' (1611) that no arrangement of equally sized spheres filling space has density greater than~$\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: no arrangement of equally sized spheres filling space has density greater than~$\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}$

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture (Hales)
nodes.statement: The Kepler conjecture was famously proven by T. Hales in 1998 \cite{Hales} and therefore we know that $\Delta_3=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}\approx0.74048$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: $\Delta_3=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}\approx0.74048$

nodes.name: Exact sphere packing constants in dimensions above 3
nodes.statement: Before now, the exact values of the sphere packing constants in all dimensions greater than~3 have been unknown.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Cohn-Elkies upper bounds nearly meet lower bounds in dimensions 8 and 24
nodes.statement: Surprisingly enough, these upper bounds and known lower bounds on $\Delta_d$ are extremely close in dimensions~$d=8$ and~$d=24$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Delta_8 = pi^4/384
nodes.statement: The main result of this paper is the proof that $$\Delta_8=\frac{\pi^4}{384}\approx 0.25367.$$ This is the density of the $E_8$-lattice sphere packing.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The sphere packing constant in dimension 8 equals $\pi^4/384$, the density of the $E_8$-lattice packing.

nodes.name: E8 lattice
nodes.statement: Recall that the $E_8$-lattice $\Lambda_8\subset\mathbb{R}^8$ is given by $$\Lambda_8=\{(x_i)\in\mathbb{Z}^8\cup(\mathbb{Z}+\textstyle\frac12\displaystyle )^8|\;\sum_{i=1}^8x_i\equiv 0\;(\mathrm{mod\;2})\}.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Characterisation of E8 as the unique even unimodular lattice of rank 8
nodes.statement: $\Lambda_8$ is the unique up to isometry positive-definite, even, unimodular lattice of rank 8.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: $\Lambda_8$ is the unique up to isometry positive-definite, even, unimodular lattice of rank 8

nodes.name: Minimal distance in E8 is sqrt 2
nodes.statement: The minimal distance between two points in $\Lambda_8$ is $\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: The minimal distance between two points in $\Lambda_8$ is $\sqrt{2}$

nodes.name: E8-lattice sphere packing
nodes.statement: The $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the packing of unit balls with centers at $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Lambda_8.$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Optimality of the E8 sphere packing in dimension 8
nodes.statement: No packing of unit balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: No packing of unit balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
also_stated_at: In this paper we prove that no packing of unit balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
nodes.label: thm: main

nodes.name: E8 is the unique periodic packing of maximal density
nodes.statement: Furthermore, our proof of Theorem~1 combined with arguments given in \cite[Section~8]{ElkiesCohn} implies that the $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the unique periodic packing of maximal density.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: the $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the unique periodic packing of maximal density

nodes.name: How far linear programming bounds are from sharp
nodes.statement: However, in general linear programming bounds are not sharp and it is an open question how big the errors of such bounds can be.

nodes.name: Asymptotic optimality of LP bounds for spherical designs
nodes.statement: It is known \cite{BRV} that the linear programming bounds for the minimal number of points in an equal weight quadrature formula on the sphere $S^d$ are asymptotically optimal up to a constant depending on $d$.
nodes.section: 2 Linear programming bounds
conclusions: the linear programming bounds for the minimal number of points in an equal weight quadrature formula on the sphere $S^d$ are asymptotically optimal up to a constant depending on $d$

nodes.name: Cohn-Elkies numerical upper bound for Delta_8
nodes.statement: For example, their upper bound for $\Delta_8$ was only $1.000001$ times greater than the lower bound, which is given by the density of the $E_8$ sphere packing.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The \emph{Fourier transform} of an $L^1$~function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is defined as $$\mathcal{F}(f)(y)=\widehat{f}(y):=\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\cdot y}\,dx,\quad y\in\mathbb{R}^d $$ where $x\cdot y=\frac12\|x\|^2+\frac12\|y\|^2-\frac12\|x-y\|^2$ is the standard scalar product in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.section: 2 Linear programming bounds

nodes.name: Schwartz function
nodes.statement: A $C^\infty$~function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is called a \emph{Schwartz function} if it tends to zero as $\|x\|\to\infty$ faster then any inverse power of $\|x\|$, and the same holds for all partial derivatives of $f$.

nodes.name: Admissible function
nodes.statement: We say that a function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is \emph{admissible} if there is a constant $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x)|$ and $|\widehat{f}(x)|$ are bounded above by a constant times $(1+|x|)^{-d-\delta}$.
nodes.section: 2 Linear programming bounds

nodes.name: Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound
nodes.statement: (Cohn, Elkies \cite{ElkiesCohn}) Suppose that $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is an admissible function, is not identically zero, and satisfies: \begin{equation} f(x)\leq 0\mbox{ for } \|x\|\geq 1\end{equation} and \begin{equation} \widehat{f}(x)\geq0\mbox{ for all } x\in\mathbb{R}^d.\end{equation} Then the density of $d$-dimensional sphere packings is bounded above by $$\frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}\cdot \frac{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{2^d\,\Gamma(\textstyle \frac{d}{2}+1)}=\frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}\cdot \mathrm{Vol}\,B_d(0,\frac 12).$$
nodes.section: 2 Linear programming bounds
assumptions: $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is an admissible function, is not identically zero
conclusions:

nodes.statement_short: If $f\le0$ outside the unit ball and $\widehat f\ge0$, every packing has density at most $f(0)/\widehat f(0)\cdot\mathrm{Vol}\,B_d(0,1/2)$.

nodes.name: Upper half-plane
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{H}$ be the upper half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Im}\,(z)>0\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Modular group Gamma(1)
nodes.statement: The modular group $\Gamma(1):=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on $\mathbb{H}$ by linear fractional transformations $$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)z:=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Principal congruence subgroup Gamma(N)
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be a positive integer. The \emph{level $N$ principal congruence subgroup} of $\Gamma(1)$ is $$\Gamma(N):=\left\{\left.\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(1)\right|\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\equiv\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\;\mathrm{mod}\;N\right\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Congruence subgroup
nodes.statement: A subgroup $\Gamma\subset\Gamma(1)$ is called a \emph{congruence subgroup} if $\Gamma(N)\subset\Gamma$ for some $N\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Congruence subgroup Gamma_0(N)
nodes.statement: An important example of a congruence subgroup is $$\Gamma_0(N):=\left\{\left.\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(1)\right|\;c\equiv0\;\mathrm{mod}\;N\right\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Automorphy factor of weight k
nodes.statement: Let $z\in\mathbb{H}$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. The \emph{automorphy factor} of weight $k$ is defined as $$j_k(z,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)):=(cz+d)^{-k}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Chain rule for the automorphy factor
nodes.statement: The automorphy factor satisfies the \emph{chain rule} $$j_k(z,\gamma_1\gamma_2)=j_k(z,\gamma_2)\,j_k(\gamma_2z,\gamma_1). $$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms
conclusions: $$j_k(z,\gamma_1\gamma_2)=j_k(z,\gamma_2)\,j_k(\gamma_2z,\gamma_1). $$

nodes.name: Slash operator
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a function on $\mathbb{H}$ and $\gamma\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. Then the \emph{slash operator} acts on $F$ by $$(F|_k\gamma)(z):=j_k(z,\gamma)\,F(\gamma z). $$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: The slash operator is a right action
nodes.statement: The chain rule implies $$F|_k\gamma_1\gamma_2=(F|_k\gamma_1)|_k\gamma_2.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms
conclusions: $$F|_k\gamma_1\gamma_2=(F|_k\gamma_1)|_k\gamma_2.$$

nodes.name: Holomorphic modular form
nodes.statement: A \emph{(holomorphic) modular form} of integer weight $k$ and congruence subgroup $\Gamma$ is a holomorphic function $f:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $f|_k\gamma=f$ for all $\gamma\in\Gamma$ and \item for each $\alpha\in\Gamma(1)$ the function $f|_k\alpha$ has Fourier expansion $$f|_k\alpha (z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_f(\alpha,\frac{n}{n_\alpha})\,e^{2\pi i \frac{n}{n_\alpha}z}$$ for some $n_\alpha\in\mathbb{N}$ and Fourier coefficients $c_f(\alpha,m)\in\mathbb{C}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let $M_k(\Gamma)$ be the space of modular forms of weight $k$ for the congruence subgroup $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Spaces of modular forms are finite dimensional

nodes.name: Eisenstein series E_k

nodes.name: Weakly-holomorphic modular form
nodes.statement: A \emph{weakly-holomorphic modular form} of integer weight $k$ and congruence subgroup $\Gamma$ is a holomorphic function $f:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $f|_k\gamma=f$ for all $\gamma\in\Gamma$, \item for each $\alpha\in\Gamma(1)$ the function $f|_k\alpha$ has Fourier expansion $$f|_k\alpha (z)=\sum_{n=n_0}^\infty c_f(\alpha,\frac{n}{n_\alpha})\,e^{2\pi i \frac{n}{n_\alpha}z}$$ for some $n_0\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $n_\alpha\in\mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Fourier coefficient c_f(n)

nodes.name: Asymptotics of the Fourier coefficients of j
nodes.statement: An important question is to find an asymptotic formula for $c_j(n)$, the $n$-th Fourier coefficient of $j$.

nodes.name: Rademacher-Petersson exact formula for the coefficients of j
nodes.statement: Using the Hardy-Ramanujan circle method \cite[p. 460 -- 461]{Rademacher38} or the non-holomorphic Poincar{\'e} series \cite{Petersson32} one can show that \begin{equation} c_j(n)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{A_k(n)}{k}\,I_1\left(\frac{4\pi \sqrt{n}}{k}\right)\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} \end{equation} where $$A_k(n)= \sum_{\substack{h\;\mathrm{mod}\;k\\(h,k)=1}} e^{\frac{-2\pi i}{k}(nh+h')},\quad hh'\equiv -1(\mbox{mod}\;k),$$ and $I_\alpha(x)$ denotes the modified Bessel function of the first kind defined as in \cite[Section~9.6]{Abramowitz}.

conclusions:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: First, we prove that $a$ is a Schwartz function. From \eqref{eqn: j Fourier asymptotic}, \eqref{eqn: varphi Fourier asymptotic}, and \eqref{eqn: D varphi} we deduce that the Fourier coefficients of $\phi_0$ satisfy $$|c_{\phi_0}(n)|\leq2\,e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.$$ Thus, there exists a positive constant $C$ such that $$|\phi_0(z)|\leq C\,e^{-2\pi \mathrm{Im}\,{z}}\qquad \mbox{for } \; \mathrm{Im}\,{z}>\frac 12.$$ We estimate the first summand in the right-hand side of \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}. For $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ we have \begin{align*}&\Bigg|\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz\Bigg|=\Bigg|\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\phi_0(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,dz\Bigg|\leq \\ &C_1\int\limits_{1/2}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2/t}\,dt\leq C_1\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2/t}\,dt=C_2\,r\,K_1(2\sqrt{2}\,\pi\,r) \end{align*} where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are some positive constants and $K_\alpha(x)$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind defined as in \cite[Section~9.6]{Abramowitz}. This estimate also holds for the second and third summand in \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}. nodes.statement: Suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Here, we repeat the arguments used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a(r) Fourier}. First we show that $b$ is a Schwartz function. We have \begin{align*} &\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz=\int\limits_{0}^{i+1}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 (z-1)}\,dz=\\ &\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,z^{-2}\,dz=\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,dz.\\ \end{align*} There exists a positive constant $C$ such that $$|\psi_S(z)|\leq C\,e^{-\pi\,\mathrm{Im}\,{z}}\quad\mbox{for }\;\mathrm{Im}\,{z}>\frac12.$$ Thus, as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a(r) Fourier} we estimate the first summand in the left-hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} $$\Bigg|\int\limits_{-1}^i \psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz \Bigg|\leq C_1\,r\,K_1(2\pi r).$$ We combine this inequality with analogous estimates for the other three summands and obtain $$|b(r)|\leq C_2\,r\,K_1(2\pi r)+C_3\,\frac{e^{-\pi(r^2+1)}}{r^2+1}.$$ Here $C_1$, $C_2$, and $C_3$ are some positive constants. Similar estimates hold for all derivatives $\frac{d^k}{d^k r} b(r)$. Now we prove that $b$ is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. We use identity~\eqref{eqn: Gaussian Fourier} and interchange contour integration in $z$ and Fourier transform in $x$. Thus we obtain \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz + \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz. \end{align*} We make the change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$ and arrive at \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{i\infty}^{i}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{0}\psi_S\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw. \end{align*} Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}--\eqref{eqn: psi S define} imply \begin{align*}\psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T ,\\ \psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S ,\\ \psi_S|_{-2}S=&\psi_I. \\ \end{align*} Therefore, we arrive at \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz \\ +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw. \end{align*} Now from~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that $$ \mathcal{F}(b)(x)=-b(x). $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: We denote the right hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} by $c(r)$. First, we check that $c(r)$ is well-defined. Then we rewrite it in the following way: $$c(r)=\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz-2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.$$ From the Fourier expansion~\eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we know that $\psi_I(z)=e^{-2\pi i z}+O(1)$ as $\mathrm{Im}\,(z)\to\infty$. By assumption $r^2>2$, hence we can deform the path of integration and write \begin{align} \int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz,\\ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align} We have \begin{align} c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ &+2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}(\psi_T(z)-\psi_I(z))\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.\nonumber \end{align} Next, we check that the functions $\psi_I,\psi_T$, and $\psi_S$ satisfy the following identity: \begin{equation} \psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I.\end{equation} Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}-\eqref{eqn: psi S define} we get \begin{align*}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S\\ =&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.\end{align*} Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$ Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore, $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h-h|_{-2}ST=\psi_I.$$ Combining \eqref{eqn: c1} and \eqref{eqn: c2} we find \begin{align*}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ &-2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ =&b(r). \end{align*}

nodes.statement: \noindent For $n\geq 0$ let $B_0^{(n)}$ and $B_{\infty}^{(n)}$ be the functions such that \begin{align*} B(t)=&B_0^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n /t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to0,\\ B(t)=&B_\infty^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{align*} We find \begin{align*}B_\infty^{(6)}(t)=&-\tfrac{12960}{\pi ^2}-\tfrac{184320}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{116640}{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{22560768}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-3\pi t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{56540160}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{869916672 }{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-5\pi t}\displaystyle\\&+t(\tfrac{8640 }{\pi }+\tfrac{2436480}{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{113011200 }{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\textstyle)-t^2(\scriptstyle518400\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle+\scriptstyle31104000\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\displaystyle) \end{align*} and $$B_0^{(6)}(t)= t^2(\tfrac{368640}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi/t}-518400\, e^{-2 \pi /t}+\tfrac{45121536 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-3 \pi/t}-31104000\, e^{-4 \pi/t}+\tfrac{1739833344 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-5 \pi/t}) .$$
nodes.statement_short: Truncated expansions B_0^(6), B_inf^(6)
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Truncation error bounded by R_0^(6), R_inf^(6)
nodes.statement: The estimates \eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 1}--\eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 5} imply that $$\left|B(t)-B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_0^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,1]$$ and $$\left|B(t)-B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in[1,\infty).$$
nodes.statement_short: Truncation error bounded by R_0^(6), R_inf^(6)
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Interval arithmetic: B(t) > 0
nodes.statement: Using interval arithmetic we verify that \begin{align*} &\left|R_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &\left|R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty),\\ &B_0^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &B_\infty^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Interval arithmetic: B(t) > 0
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Conclude (g2) from the Laplace representation
nodes.statement: Now identity \eqref{eqn: g B} implies \eqref{eqn: g2}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude (g2) from the Laplace representation

nodes.name: Prove (g3) from the special values
nodes.statement: Finally, the property \eqref{eqn: g3} readily follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: a values} and Proposition~\ref{prop: b values}. This finishes the proof of Theorems~\ref{thm: g1} and~\ref{thm: g}.
